title: Naming the Wall
passage:
Anyone who has stood in front of a paint display has noticed that the names are not descriptions. The trade calls them handles, and at Bellamy & Roe the handles for a season's forty shades are settled last, after the pigments are fixed, by two people with a spreadsheet and one rule. The rule is that a handle must not be checkable. Ferrymouth Haze cannot be held up beside a ferrymouth haze and found wrong; Tomato can, and a customer who grows tomatoes will say so at the counter. So the winners drift toward places nobody has been and weather nobody has photographed. The occasional literal name survives only because the thing it borrows from comes in enough versions to swallow the error — brick, ash, sand.
— Odile Brennan, design notebook

questions.prompt: What are we told about the rule that Bellamy & Roe applies when naming a shade?

options.text: That a name is acceptable as long as the thing it borrows from comes in many versions.
That a name is chosen because no buyer is in a position to prove it inaccurate.
That a name works best when it describes the shade closely enough to be recognized.
That a name is kept only if it can be defended against the trade's own color standards.

questions.rationale: TYPE-001 direct detail, joining the stated rule to the worked example that explains it. The text gives the rule as 'a handle must not be checkable' and then shows what that means in practice: Ferrymouth Haze 'cannot be held up beside a ferrymouth haze and found wrong', whereas Tomato can, and a customer who grows tomatoes 'will say so at the counter'. B paraphrases that. A = the exception overgeneralized into the rule: the passage does say a name can borrow from something that 'comes in enough versions to swallow the error', but it says that only of 'the occasional literal name' — brick, ash, sand — as the reason a rare exception gets through, not as the rule the team applies. It also does not fit the winning names, which borrow from 'places nobody has been and weather nobody has photographed' rather than from many-versioned things. C = the naive general belief the passage opens by denying ('the names are not descriptions'); it is the position a reader brings to the text rather than one the text supports, and the whole rule works the other way around. D = surface_word_match on 'the trade' with the wrong auditor: the passage's test is whether a customer can catch the name out, not whether the name survives an industry color standard, and no such standard is mentioned anywhere. Hedge balance: all four options are flat, confident claims and the key is the specific one, so 'pick the qualified answer' does not locate it; D carries an absolutizer ('only') but so does the key ('no buyer'), so 'avoid the absolute-sounding option' does not separate them either; and the key is not the longest option (B is the shortest by character count, though C is one word shorter). A and B both describe a name as insulated from being caught out while C and D make it answerable to an outside check, so the key is not the odd one out on shape alone.
